blocks.content: By default, a container can use as much CPU and memory as the host has available, on a shared host, that is a real risk. Resource limits put a hard, enforced ceiling on what any one container can consume.

--memory sets a hard ceiling on how much RAM a container can use, enforced by the same cgroups mechanism introduced in the Containerization topic, this is not a soft suggestion, the kernel actively enforces it.

blocks.alt: A real, kernel-enforced ceiling on memory usage

blocks.content: --cpus similarly caps how much CPU time a container can consume, expressed as a number of cores, --cpus=1.5 means this container can never use more than one and a half CPU cores' worth of processing time, regardless of how many cores the host actually has.

blocks.alt: A cap expressed directly in CPU cores

blocks.content: 3. What Happens When a Container Exceeds Its Memory Limit
blocks.text: 3. What Happens When a Container Exceeds Its Memory Limit

blocks.content: Exceeding a CPU limit just means the container is throttled, slowed down. Exceeding a memory limit is more severe, the kernel's out-of-memory killer (OOM killer) terminates the offending process outright, this is a hard failure, not a graceful slowdown, worth knowing when debugging an unexpectedly dying container.

blocks.alt: A memory limit breach ends in a hard kill, not a slowdown

blocks.content:
docker inspect mycontainer --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}'
# true, if the container was killed for exceeding its memory limit

code.content:
docker inspect mycontainer --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}'
# true, if the container was killed for exceeding its memory limit

codes.bash:
docker inspect mycontainer --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}'
# true, if the container was killed for exceeding its memory limit

blocks.content: 4. The Problem Without Any Limits: Noisy Neighbors
blocks.text: 4. The Problem Without Any Limits: Noisy Neighbors

blocks.content: On a host running several containers, one runaway or misbehaving container with no limits can consume enough CPU or memory to starve every other container sharing that host, an entirely avoidable failure mode with no relation to what those other containers are actually doing wrong.

blocks.alt: One unlimited container can starve everything else on the host

blocks.content: 5. Why This Matters More on Shared Infrastructure
blocks.text: 5. Why This Matters More on Shared Infrastructure

blocks.content: The more containers sharing one host, the more resource limits stop being optional and start being a basic operational requirement, they are what makes every container's behavior predictable and isolated from its neighbors' resource usage, not just its filesystem and process namespace.

blocks.alt: Predictability for every container sharing a host

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: --memory and --cpus put real, kernel-enforced ceilings on a container's resource usage, exceeding the memory limit results in a hard OOM kill.
Without limits, one misbehaving container can starve every other container on a shared host, resource limits are what makes multi-tenant hosting predictable.
